title: Unmatched: Fulfillment and delivery: exceeding customer expectations (panel)
title_note: Not yet matched to an agenda session. Moderator is a co-founder/CEO of a fulfilment company (name unclear in the recording); guests introduced as Thomas Stevens, General Manager of Retail at DoorDash, and Dylan (surname unclear) of a 180-year-old bedding brand transcribed as “Mansutan”.
transcript_note: Assembled from two pastes: the opening of the session, then a gap, then the remainder. Song lyrics picked up after the session ended were removed.
takeaways: Moderator's framing: design beats spend; treat inventory placement as a strategy; close the gap between the delivery promise made and what is actually delivered.
Retailers already stock the best SKUs for their market, so DoorDash puts items in its own fulfilment nodes mainly for late-night demand or fast movers that stores struggle to keep in stock.
The bedding brand plans capacity from 30-day trailing order concentration and saturates target markets (e.g. Phoenix); its oversized boxes make shipping costly, so pricing is built around that.
Automate only once a process is proven and tied to a real customer problem; go high-touch first to learn where the pain is. DoorDash has launched drone delivery with Lowe's in Charlotte.
Align marketing promises with actual operations: DoorDash sets advertised delivery times each quarter from real delivery data; the bedding brand uses NPS as its shared north star.
Advice: stop copying competitors, and stop communicating with customers the way you used to.

title: Unmatched: Loyalty and membership panel
title_note: Not yet matched to an agenda session. Panelists include the General Manager of Walmart+ (first name transcribed as Deepak) and the President of The UPS Store (first name Brad), plus a third panelist whose name and company are unclear (discusses pros vs DIY customers), with a female moderator.
takeaways: Loyalty programs are getting more spend but less engagement: about half of points are never redeemed and many members want to leave; experiences now beat financial rewards as the reason to join.
Walmart+ ($98/year, over a dozen benefits) aims to be an “essential membership” rather than a points program; members shop 3x more often and spend 4x more than non-members.
Walmart+ prioritises high-uncertainty, high-reward experiments and uses early proxy metrics (benefit activation, using several benefits early) to predict retention.
The UPS Store: customer experience never exceeds that of the people delivering it; RFID tracking was rolled out to remove friction, not to chase technology.
Use counter-metrics so optimising one KPI doesn't damage the wider experience.
transcript_note: Audio for parts of the third panelist's answers is unclear.

title: Unmatched: TikTok Shop session
title_note: Not yet matched to an agenda session. Moderator Neil; speakers Patrick (TikTok Shop) and Sarah, founder of Beachwaver (surnames not clear in the recording).
takeaways: TikTok Shop launched in the US three years ago; shopping starts with discovery rather than search, though there were over 100 billion shopping-intent searches last year. Best Buy is launching soon with 10,000+ products.
Live selling has no time limit (unlike a 10-minute QVC slot), so founders can educate and entertain; Beachwaver has run 465 live streams since January 2024.
Community drives repeat purchase and product ideas: hundreds of Beachwaver customers have ordered 30+ times, and a cow-print design requested by the community was its fastest sellout.
Advice: big brands should keep brand principles but be flexible in execution and give creators freedom; be consistent, since TikTok Shop is an always-on channel, not a one-off viral moment.

title: Unmatched: AI in operations panel (AWS, OpenAI, Sears)
title_note: Not yet matched to an agenda session. Moderator Aparna (AWS, retail, restaurants and consumer goods business development); panelists Jack (OpenAI, consumer industries) and Srini (CEO of a Sears technology business unit). Surnames unclear in the recording.
takeaways: OpenAI: about 1.5 billion shopping-related queries a week on ChatGPT; getting product data and PDPs properly enriched is table stakes for agentic commerce; virtual try-on inside ChatGPT is coming.

Sears' AI agent “Chris” acts as “CEO of the service order”: a live video/voice assistant diagnoses appliance problems before the technician visit, predicts parts, routes jobs by expected profitability and offers protection plans (shown in a live demo).

Sears' contact centre handles about 2 million calls with AI (“Samantha”); cost per call fell from about $8 to around 21 cents, and every call can be analysed to drive improvements. Focus on value per outcome, not token cost.
Chris also mapped and now runs Sears' capital approval (CapCom) process, briefing presenters beforehand and sitting in board meetings as a non-voting participant; humans still make the decision.
Agent-to-agent orchestration (e.g. Lowe's associate assistant expanding to customers) and observability are key; spend on change management alongside AI.
transcript_note: Includes a recorded and a live demo, so parts are the AI agent's own speech.

title: Unmatched: Live shopping and social commerce sessions
title_note: Not yet matched to an agenda session. Appears to be several back-to-back conversations with one host: the founder of a European patches/supplements brand, a QVC executive (social/TikTok), and the founder-CEO of Canvas Beauty. Names unclear in the recording.
takeaways: Patches brand: educate, educate, educate; test products for one to three months and drop what doesn't work; live streams run up to 8 hours a day in the US, and high-energy, urgent selling worked better in the US than the UK.

QVC treats TikTok as a discovery enabler, not a competitor: a separate start-up-style team, TikTok-only hosts and five TikTok studios brought about 1 million new customers in 2025; launched a TikTok-exclusive apparel brand.
Canvas Beauty: people buy into a movement, not a product; sell aspiration; owning manufacturing allows a 14-day concept-to-launch turnaround; set a record with a $2.6 million TikTok live.
Common advice: be authentic and consistent, test relentlessly, and be brand-authentic but platform-native.

title: Unmatched: Commerce platform and conversion rate talk (Brian Gillespie)
title_note: Not yet matched to an agenda session. Short talk by Brian Gillespie (company not stated in the recording); the recording starts partway through.
takeaways: Replatforming every few years rarely fixes the real problems, which are usually processes and data.
Conversion rate is a misleading hero metric: cutting top-of-funnel traffic can raise it while hurting long-term health, and B2B buyers visit many times before buying.
AI agents don't respond to countdown timers or homepage merchandising; they check inventory and price, so sites must work for bots without a storefront.

title: Unmatched: Consumer trends interactive roundtable
title_note: Not yet matched to an agenda session. Interactive table-discussion session led by a market-research presenter (company not stated), with attendees from Dollar Tree, Journeys, Living Spaces and others.
takeaways: Income polarisation: growth is shifting to $100K+ households (27% of consumers control 62% of disposable income); channel growth is at the extremes while department stores decline.

AI referrals grew 376% since January 2025 (about 2–3% of traffic); impact is highest in beauty and personal care (47%) and lowest in soft drinks; AI rewards the brand that best answers the shopper's question.
Friends and family remain the most trusted source (65%); communities increasingly shape demand.
Table answers: Dollar Tree's multi-price strategy attracts higher-income shoppers; brands must serve both core and new customers.

title: Unmatched: Agentic commerce fireside chat (Anthropic)
title_note: Not yet matched to an agenda session. Interview with an Anthropic speaker on Claude and agentic commerce; names unclear in the recording.
takeaways: Three modalities of agentic commerce: discovery on Claude (without owning checkout), Claude agents purchasing on merchant sites, and merchants' own agents.
Trust rests on privacy, accuracy and being unbiased; Anthropic says there is no advertising and no paid ranking in Claude.
To be surfaced: allow agents via robots.txt and your CDN, keep product data in HTML with full descriptions and prices, and keep it current.
Claude Commerce Agent, an open-source reference for merchant agents, was launched this month; merchants report about 35% larger carts and 60% higher conversion. Smaller models suit most use cases.

title: Unmatched: Amazon Prime fireside chat
title_note: Not yet matched to an agenda session. Interview with Jameel (surname transcribed as Gani), who leads Amazon Prime worldwide; interviewer not named in the recording.
takeaways: Prime has over 200 million paid members in 27 countries; it is a paid membership, not a loyalty program or a loss leader, and every unit shipped must be contribution-profit accretive.
Grocery and everyday essentials: perishable customers up 50% and same/next-day items up 40% in the first half of the year; the fastest speeds have the lowest cost to serve.
Price has barely risen: $79 in 2005 would be $133 adjusted for inflation versus $139 today, for far more selection and speed.
Advice: show loyalty to the customer from day one, and never build a business model on breakage.

title: Unmatched: Agentic commerce session (AWS, Anthropic, Coresight Research)
title_note: Not yet matched to an agenda session. A presentation by Justin (AWS, retail and consumer goods), a presentation by Marina (heads partnerships at Anthropic; name partly unclear), then a panel moderated by Deborah Weinswig (Founder & CEO, Coresight Research).
takeaways: AWS: most retailers are still held back by fragmented data (multiple ERPs, separate commerce systems); agentic AI is already live at Amazon in Rufus/Alexa for Shopping, Buy for Me, advertising and the internal tool Amazon Quick.

Anthropic: three modalities of agentic commerce; the open-source Claude Commerce Agent covers consumer-facing, merchandising and supply-chain agents, with about 35% larger carts and 60% higher conversion reported.
Coresight: a 75% increase in agentic build for commerce in the last 90 days; AI leadership roles are increasingly reporting to the CEO.
Retailer concerns from the AI council: connecting stores and e-commerce, proving the value of AI, supply chain, cybersecurity and change management; many retailers are hiring, not cutting.
Advice: ask to see AI working with real customers, invest in change management, and keep the customer at the centre.

title: Unmatched: Estée Lauder Companies keynote
title_note: Not yet matched to an agenda session. Tara Simon, President of the Americas, and Lisa Sequino, President of MAC (title transcribed as “President of Makeup Bluster”), The Estée Lauder Companies; interviewed by Jessica Matlin, founder and host of Fat Mascara (names as introduced on stage).
takeaways: MAC launched at Sephora in nine months instead of the usual 18–24 by throwing out the rule book; the launch was treated as a cultural moment (campaign by Nicola Formichetti, a fast-turnaround billboard in Times Square).
ELC is now on Amazon and TikTok Shop; channels feed each other (e.g. a TikTok Shop Super Brand Day for Clinique Black Honey lifted sales at Ulta and Amazon within hours).
Brand equity and reach aren't mutually exclusive: keep brand codes but be flexible per channel; Kilian Paris's $150 cocktails collection sold out on Sephora.com in 72 hours.
Leadership: challenger mindset, speed without asking permission, being direct, and “phone a friend” — nobody has all the answers.
